summary:
Gentius was the last attested king of the Illyrian Labeatan dynasty, ruling from 181 to 168 BC from Scodra (modern Shkodër, Albania). Early in his reign, several peoples and cities broke away from his authority, while relations with Rome deteriorated. He strengthened his kingdom’s finances and navy, and built an army reported to number 15,000.

Initially allied with Rome against Macedon, Gentius switched sides in 169 BC and joined Perseus of Macedon. After receiving a promised subsidy, he arrested Roman envoys and attacked Roman-aligned cities. Rome responded in 168 BC: the forces of Lucius Anicius Gallus defeated Gentius’s army and captured Scodra within about a month. Gentius surrendered and was taken to Rome, then held at Iguvium; the date of his death is unknown.

Rome dissolved the Illyrian kingdom and divided its territory into three administrative districts. Some communities retained local autonomy but paid reduced taxes to Rome, while others were punished and looted. The article also notes that Gentius’s name may be related to the Albanian name Gjin, though this is uncertain; the gentian plant genus is named in his honor. He is commemorated on Albanian currency.
unsupportedClaims: Several cities broke away early in Gentius’s reign. The points name two peoples that declared independence early and one city that abandoned him at an unspecified time before his defeat.
Gentius built the army of 15,000. The points say he had and assembled an army, not that he raised it.
Gentius received the promised subsidy before arresting the Roman envoys. He received only a ten-talent advance, and Perseus withheld the rest after the arrests.
